draft.title: Does measured adaptation close the gap?
draft.verdict: Adapting a pretrained generator to measured radar has not yet been shown to compensate for simulator mismatch. The synthetic rehearsal raised detector mean AP from 66.46% to 70.46%, but triggered a copying warning. The corrected transfer pilot completed only zero mismatch, where generated augmentation scored 48.51% against raw simulation’s 60.55%. RADIal-sized pretraining is configured and recipe checks are saved, but the measured detector comparison remains open.

terms.meaning: Detection precision across score thresholds, averaged over target classes. Higher is better.
Continuing a pretrained generator’s learning on the measured training examples.
Highest minus lowest score across runs with different random starting points.
A moving average of model weights used to generate samples.
Difference between bright and faint map values, measured here between specified percentiles.
A setting that changes the noise levels used during diffusion training and sampling.

sections.heading: Define the comparison
sections.takeaway: The intended test asks whether fine-tuned generation stays useful when raw simulator augmentation becomes worse as simulator mismatch grows.
sections.body: The design compares measured training data alone, measured data plus raw simulated scenes, and measured data plus generated scenes after adaptation. Each comparison should use the same measured subset, held-out recordings and added-data budget, with three random seeds. The key evidence would be different responses to simulator quality, rather than a gain against measured data alone. The design originally listed three simulator levels, while the current scene pipeline implements engineer and fitted variants.

excerpts.heading: Specify the success pattern
excerpts.notice: Lines 142-146 define the proposed mechanism and its failure pattern. These are experimental intentions, not saved measured results.

excerpts.heading: Keep variants separate
excerpts.notice: Line 397 exposes two variants. Lines 391-394 load fitted settings separately, so the engineer variant does not inherit calibration from measured data.

sections.heading: Limit the rehearsal
sections.takeaway: The earlier augmentation gain establishes a working synthetic experiment, but its copying check limits what that gain proves.
sections.body: In the saved 64×64 experiment, the examples called real are simulator-generated reference sequences. Adding 8,000 generated sequences to 2,000 reference sequences improved mean AP by 4.00 percentage points, exceeding the 1.82-point comparison spread across three seeds. Detectors trained for 3,000 steps and were evaluated on 512 held-out sequences. A separate check made 128 requests from training labels and 128 from held-out labels. Generated maps were substantially closer to their matching training examples, so the gain cannot establish that the generator learned transferable variation.

excerpts.heading: Pass the gain rule
excerpts.notice: The gain at line 122 exceeds the comparison bar at line 123. The saved helps value concerns the synthetic target-class experiment.

excerpts.heading: Trigger the copying warning
excerpts.notice: Line 8 gives a training-to-held-out distance ratio of 0.715. The check flags ratios below 0.8, explaining the true value at line 9.

excerpts.heading: Compare matching examples
excerpts.notice: Lines 50-51 compare generated sequences with examples carrying the same labels. Line 60 applies a distance threshold, so this is a copying warning rather than proof of exact duplication.

sections.heading: Read the pilot
sections.takeaway: The corrected simulator-to-simulator pilot saved only the zero-offset point, where raw simulation outperformed generated augmentation.
sections.body: The pilot planned target-brightness offsets of 0, 4, 8 and 16 dB, but the supplied result contains only 0 dB. Its reference pool has 200 simulated sequences, with 6,000 sequences allocated to generator pretraining. Both augmentation arms add 800 sequences and are tested on 400 reference sequences. Across three detector seeds, reference-only mean AP is 46.20%, raw simulation reaches 60.55%, and generated augmentation reaches 48.51%, with a 12.47-point spread for the generated arm. The archive index identifies this as the corrected point after an invalid EMA run, so the design note’s running curve is not a completed mismatch study.

excerpts.heading: Finish only zero mismatch
excerpts.notice: Lines 6-8 mark the 0 dB point complete. Lines 13-14 give equal augmentation counts, making pool size an unlikely explanation for the difference.

excerpts.heading: Lose to raw simulation
excerpts.notice: Line 69 records raw simulation’s mean of 0.6055. Line 96 records generated augmentation’s 0.4851, and line 97 shows its larger run-to-run spread.

sections.heading: Prepare larger scenes
sections.takeaway: The current pipeline prepares eight-frame 512×256 generator pretraining, but its saved checks measure simulator resemblance rather than measured transfer.
sections.body: Simulator fitting uses training recordings only, and its saved statistics retain differences from measured radar. For example, fitted vehicle prominence is 20.03 dB above the surrounding range background, compared with 23.98 dB in measured maps. The generator recipe check then compares generated scenes with engineer-simulator scenes. After 20 epochs, shift 16 produces a 50.00 dB dynamic range, closer to the simulator’s 57.20 dB than shift 4’s 42.06 dB. Both pretraining configurations select shift 16 and 80 epochs, but these configuration values do not establish completed pretraining or adaptation.

excerpts.heading: Record measured calibration
excerpts.notice: Line 2 restricts the fit to training recordings. Line 9 gives measured vehicle prominence, while line 18 shows that the current engineer simulator’s vehicles are fainter, unlike the older brightness-gap account.

excerpts.heading: Recover more brightness spread
excerpts.notice: Line 97 gives the shift-16 generated dynamic range after 20 epochs. Line 104 gives its simulator reference, leaving about 7.20 dB of missing spread.

excerpts.heading: Select the pretraining recipe
excerpts.notice: Lines 8-10 choose eight frames at 512×256. Lines 24 and 32 select shift 16 and 80 epochs, which define the next training budget rather than a result.

sections.heading: Complete measured adaptation
sections.takeaway: The current launcher ends at simulator pretraining, leaving measured adaptation, sample checks and detector evaluation to be made concrete.
sections.body: The launcher trains engineer then fitted variants, resumes each from last.pt, and writes STAGE_DONE after training returns successfully. No measured-adaptation configuration or RADIal detector result appears among the current scripts and supplied results, and local pretraining logs are absent. The training loop already supports starting a new run from train.init_from, while resume also restores optimizer state and training counters. Scene conditioning accepts per-frame vehicle positions and presence rather than the rehearsal’s target classes, so the measured detector task still needs an explicit definition. Short adaptation runs also need deliberate weight selection because slowly updated EMA weights can retain much of their starting state.

excerpts.heading: Stop after simulator training
excerpts.notice: Line 18 resumes existing checkpoints, and line 22 marks each stage done. There is no measured fine-tuning or detector invocation after either variant.

excerpts.heading: Start from pretrained weights
excerpts.notice: Line 245 enables a new run from init_from only when no resume state is loaded. Lines 250-254 choose averaged or raw starting weights before creating the new EMA.

excerpts.heading: Check averaging carryover
excerpts.notice: Line 307 warns when over 10% of initial weights remain in the estimated EMA. Lines 309-310 explain why raw sampling or faster averaging can matter for short runs.

notebook.title: Does measured adaptation close the gap?
notebook.verdict: Measured adaptation has not been shown to compensate for simulator mismatch. A generator trained from scratch raised synthetic target-class mean AP from 66.46% to 70.46%, with a copying warning. A separate simulator pilot saved only zero brightness offset, where generated additions scored 48.51% against raw simulation’s 60.55%. Larger-scene recipe checks are saved, but the measured RADIal detector comparison is still missing.

terms.meaning: Area under the precision-recall curve, averaged over target classes. Higher is better.
Continuing a pretrained generator’s learning on measured training examples.
Highest minus lowest score across runs with different random starting points.
An exponential moving average of model weights, used for generation.
Here, the difference between the 99.9th and 0.1st percentile map values.
A setting that changes how much noise the generator learns to remove.
Decibels, a logarithmic scale for comparing radar power.
Saved model weights and training state that can start or continue a run.

sections.heading: Compare added data
sections.takeaway: The test needs to show that adaptation protects detector performance when extra raw simulator data becomes less useful.
sections.body: For each simulator variant, compare measured training sequences alone, those sequences plus raw simulation, and those sequences plus generation after fine-tuning. The design also proposes generation without fine-tuning to isolate what adaptation contributes. Keep the measured subset, held-out recordings, added sequence count and detector training budget fixed, with three random seeds. The current code exposes engineer settings without measured fitting and fitted settings calibrated on measured training recordings, while the design describes three simulator levels. Success requires a difference in how raw simulation and adapted generation respond to mismatch, which the saved zero-offset pilot cannot establish.

excerpts.heading: Define the success pattern
excerpts.notice: Lines 142-146 propose raw simulation worsening while adapted generation stays useful. This is the intended test, not a saved measured result.

excerpts.heading: Separate simulator settings
excerpts.notice: Line 397 exposes engineer and fitted variants. Lines 391-394 load fitted settings separately, keeping measured calibration out of the engineer variant.

sections.heading: Bound the rehearsal
sections.takeaway: The synthetic gain passes its saved comparison rule, but neither pretrained adaptation nor transferable variation is established.
sections.body: The 64×64 rehearsal trained the generator from scratch on 2,000 simulator sequences, rather than adapting pretrained weights to recordings. Adding 8,000 generated sequences raised mean AP from 66.46% to 70.46%, with detectors trained for 3,000 steps and evaluated on 512 held-out simulator sequences. A detection must have the correct target class and lie within two map bins of its labelled position, and the 4.00-point gain exceeds the larger seed spread of the compared runs, 1.82 points. The rule also checks that using all 20,000 simulator training sequences improves the baseline beyond run variation before calling the augmentation test informative. Separately, 128 requests from training labels and 128 from held-out labels produced median normalized map distances of 0.795 and 1.112 to their matching examples, triggering the copying warning.

excerpts.heading: Pass the gain rule
excerpts.notice: Line 122 saves a gain of 0.0400, or 4.00 percentage points, against line 123’s 1.82-point bar. Line 121 records that the full-data comparison leaves enough room for improvement.

excerpts.heading: Flag closer training matches
excerpts.notice: Line 8’s distance ratio is 0.715, below the check’s 0.8 threshold. Generated sequences match training examples more closely than held-out examples.

excerpts.heading: Compare matching examples
excerpts.notice: Lines 50-51 compare generation with examples carrying the requested labels. Line 60 applies the ratio threshold, which flags a copying concern without proving exact duplication.

sections.heading: Zero offset loses
sections.takeaway: At the pilot’s only saved brightness offset, adding raw simulation beats adding generated sequences.
sections.body: The design planned offsets of 0, 4, 8 and 16 dB between simulator target brightness and a simulated reference world, but the result contains only 0 dB. It records 200 reference training sequences and 6,000 simulator sequences for generator pretraining, with 800 added sequences in each detector comparison. After 2,500 detector training steps, mean AP across three seeds on 400 reference test sequences is 46.20% with reference data alone, 60.55% with raw simulation and 48.51% with generation. The generated comparison’s 12.47-point seed spread is also larger than raw simulation’s 3.46-point spread. The archive index identifies this as the corrected completed point after an invalid EMA run, and the missing nonzero offsets leave the proposed mismatch trend untested.

excerpts.heading: Save zero offset
excerpts.notice: Lines 6-8 mark only the 0 dB point complete. Lines 13-14 record equal additions of 800 sequences, and lines 15-16 fix the detector budget and test count.

excerpts.heading: Favor raw simulation
excerpts.notice: Lines 69 and 96 give mean AP of 60.55% with raw simulation and 48.51% with generation. Lines 70 and 97 give their respective seed spreads.

sections.heading: Check scene readiness
sections.takeaway: The saved larger-scene checks justify a training recipe, but they compare generation with simulation rather than measured detector performance.
sections.body: Calibration uses measured training recordings only, and the fitted simulator’s vehicles remain 20.03 dB above surrounding range background against measured vehicles’ 23.98 dB. The current engineer value is 14.84 dB, so the older design note’s account of overly bright targets belongs to an earlier simulator. The recipe evaluation uses eight generated sequences and eight separate held-out engineer-simulator sequences, each containing eight 512×256 frames. After 20 epochs, schedule shift 16 produces a 50.00 dB dynamic range against the simulator’s 57.20 dB, closer than shift 4’s 42.06 dB but still short by 7.20 dB. Both pretraining configurations select shift 16 and 80 epochs, which specify a budget rather than prove that training finished.

excerpts.heading: Retain a contrast gap
excerpts.notice: Line 9 gives measured vehicle prominence of 23.98 dB. Lines 18 and 40 give engineer and fitted values of 14.84 and 20.03 dB, leaving fitted vehicles 3.95 dB below the measured value.

excerpts.heading: Recover brightness spread
excerpts.notice: Lines 91-95 identify shift 16 after 20 epochs. Lines 97 and 104 give generated and simulator dynamic ranges of 50.00 and 57.20 dB, measured between the same percentiles.

excerpts.heading: Choose the training budget
excerpts.notice: Lines 8-10 set eight frames at 512×256. Lines 24 and 32 select schedule shift 16 and 80 epochs, not a completed training result.

sections.heading: Finish measured adaptation
sections.takeaway: The launcher stops at simulator pretraining, while measured fine-tuning and detector evaluation still need concrete configurations and saved outputs.
sections.body: The launcher trains engineer then fitted variants, continues from last.pt when present, and writes STAGE_DONE after each training command succeeds. This checkout has neither local checkpoint nor log directories, and its current configurations and scripts provide no measured adaptation run or measured detector result. The training loop can start from pretrained weights through train.init_from with a fresh optimizer, whereas resume restores optimizer state and training counters. Scene inputs request per-frame vehicle positions and presence rather than the rehearsal’s target classes, so the measured detector task and matching rule need to be specified. Short adaptation runs also need an explicit raw or EMA weight choice because the averaging estimate can retain substantial starting weights, and its warning uses the configured full budget rather than actual completed updates.

excerpts.heading: End at simulator training
excerpts.notice: Line 18 continues an existing checkpoint, and line 22 writes the completion marker after success. The launcher invokes no measured adaptation or detector evaluation.

excerpts.heading: Load pretrained weights
excerpts.notice: Line 245 starts from init_from only without a resume state. Lines 250-254 select EMA weights by default or raw weights explicitly before line 261 creates the new average.

excerpts.heading: Estimate averaging carryover
excerpts.notice: Line 306 estimates starting-weight retention using configured epochs times loader length. Line 307 warns above 10%, so this warning does not verify the checkpoint’s actual completed updates.
